Interesting. I wonder what specifically increases the chance of death. There are many factors involved, and automotive safety systems are a pet fascination of mine.
If I had to pull a wild guess out of my butt, I'd say that the extra body mass makes it more difficult to endure the fairly extreme accelerations of a crash.

Well in a crash, there's 3 collisions.

1- the vehicle

2- the contents of the vehicle, including you.

3- the contents of your body.

An obese/overweight person will experience much greater forces in collisions 2 & 3 than normal and underweight people. The safety measures are only tested to around 200lbs, IIRC. So, it's insanity to think that going over the tested threshold by 100+ pounds will result in anything other than greater injuries or even a greater chance of death.

That's just the limits of the human body. That's not even taking into account how the car itself would react to 250+ lbs impacting the interior. Changing saftey measure to accommodate persons of a greater mass could also result in greater injuries to average/smaller people as well.

You know your automotive safety :)

I didn't know the 200 lb testing limit, thanks for bringing that up. Anyone heavier would cause sub-optimal performance of the seatbelt tension limiters and airbag. I suspect that the fat in front of the torso is harmful because it reduces the space for deceleration, rather than acting to absorb some of the impact. Back fat would be even worse, pushing the person farther forward in the seat and increasing their momentum.

I also wouldn't be surprised if they had a worse recovery rate from otherwise identical injuries.

Thank you! According to Wikipedia, the biggest crash test dummy they use is 6'2 and 223lbs. So, even though it's tested to that weight, it's dispersed over a greater area than the typical fatty occupies.

Fat definitely takes the effectiveness out of airbags and seatbelts. You're supposed to have 10" minimum between your chest and the steering wheel (and keep your hands clear of the center). Think of how many stories of obeasts there's been where their gut is touching the wheel, or they have it shoved all the way up so it's aimed at their face. Airbags are violent enough under ideal circumstances. They can break bones at that 10" range. Shove a fatty into the 5" range, and they'll be seriously injured by it. Normal people have had bones broken by properly functioning air bags.

Seatbelts, even if the excess weight doesn't break them, can only stop so much. You want to stop the body from accelerating ASAP. Fat compresses, so their bodies will continue to travel until they can't be squished anymore. Greater weight+longer distance to stop=more force exerted against the seatbelt to stop. It can rupture organs, cause internal bleeding, or at the very least leave some awful bruising. A fully extended belt also makes it more likely to fail.
